text:
Legal framework for Internet Shutdown in India

Context: During the "Chalo Sansad" protest organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), Mobile Internet Service were shut down in parts of Central Delhi.

Provisions:

~Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunication Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, Telecommunication services may be suspended.

~Suspension can be ordered only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing.

~Orders must be reasoned, published, geographically and temporarily limited and consider whether less restrictive measures are sufficient.

Under the 2024 Rules, a suspension order cannot remain in force for more than 15 days.

Supreme Court Guidelines:

~In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court linked Internet access with freedoms under Articles 19(1) (a) and 19(1)(g).

~Shutdowns must satisfy necessity and proportionality, be the least restrictive measures, and remain open to judicial review.

Suspension can be challenged in court?
Yes. Under Article 226 before a High Court and Article 32 before the Supreme Court.

India's Position:
India recorded about 24 Internet shutdowns in 2026 till July 22; Jammu & Kashmir has recorded the highest cumulative number since 2012.

Pic created by AI

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI model, disclosed this week that it caught and banned an Iran-linked account that spent from December 2025 through August 2026 building what its own threat report calls “𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘨𝘦𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘩𝘢𝘯𝘥𝘣𝘰𝘰𝘬𝘴…𝘵𝘰 𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘧𝘺 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘤𝘬 𝘯𝘢𝘷𝘢𝘭 𝘱𝘰𝘴𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘣𝘢𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘰𝘯 𝘰𝘱𝘦𝘯-𝘴𝘰𝘶𝘳𝘤𝘦 𝘪𝘯𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘮𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯.” The target: American warships operating in the Middle East.

The operation was methodical. Investigators found the account had compiled ship and aircraft 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐬, pulled service members' faces from public military photographs, queried commercial satellite imagery to pinpoint exact locations, and cataloged public websites that track Navy movements in real time. It also dug into known 𝐰𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐍𝐚𝐯𝐲 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐛𝐨𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐬𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐬 — the kind of detail that turns open-source snooping into an actual targeting package.

Anthropic says it shut the account down, built new detection tools to catch the next one, and handed everything over to the Pentagon and other U.S. government agencies before Tehran could turn any of it into a real-world attack. The same 154-page threat report flagged a separate Yemeni cell using Claude to build a guided missile targeting system — proof this wasn't a one-off.

Iran's proxies have been gutted since the war ended and its economy is in shambles, but this is the adaptation: a regime that can no longer fight the U.S. Navy conventionally is trying to outsource the reconnaissance to a public AI model instead. text:
These bonds exist to be destroyed. After the 2008 crash, regulators wanted banks to hold capital that could absorb losses without a taxpayer bailout, so Additional Tier-1 bonds were built with a trigger: if the bank gets into trouble, they can be written down to nothing while the bank keeps running. That is not a malfunction, it is the purpose. Which is why the law restricts who can be sold one.
Credit Suisse made it worse. When Swiss regulators wiped $17 billion of AT-1 bonds in March 2023, shareholders still walked away with roughly $3.2 billion from the UBS rescue. Bondholders are meant to rank above shareholders. That order was inverted, and lawsuits followed in several countries.
India has seen this before. In March 2020, Yes Bank’s AT-1 bonds worth ₹8,415 crore were written off, and many had reached retail investors who believed they were buying something close to a fixed deposit. The Bombay High Court later set that write-off aside, the Supreme Court stayed the order, and six years on it is still unresolved.
There are fixes. Reclassifying a customer as a professional or expert investor should require separate written consent on its own document, not a clause buried in a bundle. Banks should have to hand over a plain-language sheet naming the worst case. And regulators should audit classifications rather than wait for complaints, because by the time a complaint exists the money is gone.
So here is the question worth sitting with. If the person selling you a financial product also decides how much legal protection you get from it, what exactly is your signature agreeing to?
Sources: CNBC-TV18, Business Standard, PTI, Gulf News, Bloomberg, DFSA notifications, HDFC Bank exchange filings.

text:
A man in Bangalore bought 3 tickets for an afternoon film.He got to his seat on time. 

Then the cinema played 25 minutes of advertisements before the film began.

Because of that, the film finished late. He had work calls booked afterwards. He had to cancel them.

So he took the biggest cinema chain in the country to court.

His name is Abhishek M R.

He is a lawyer in Bangalore. He was 31 at the time.

The date was 26th December 2023. The film was Sam Bahadur. The cinema was a PVR INOX.

His ticket said the show would begin at a certain time. It did not begin at that time.

What played first was 25 minutes of commercials. Not trailers for other films. Advertisements.

Now, everybody has sat through this. You reach the hall on time, and then you sit in the dark watching advertisements while the film waits. It is so normal that nobody even thinks of it as a problem any more.

He thought it was a problem.

He filed a case at the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission in Bangalore.

His argument was simple. He had paid for a service. That service was advertised to start at a fixed time. It did not start at that time. His own time was taken from him without his agreement, and it cost him his work calls.

The cinema chain defended itself. It said the law requires cinemas to play about 10 minutes of public service announcements before a film, so some delay cannot be helped.

The commission accepted that 10 minutes may be required.

It did not accept that 10 minutes explains 25.

The order went against the company.

It was told to pay him 20,000 rupees as damages, and 8,000 rupees towards the cost of fighting the case. It was also told to pay 1 lakh rupees to the Consumer Welfare Fund, which is a government fund for consumer protection work.

The wording of the judgement is the part worth remembering.

The commission wrote that in the new era, time is considered as money, and each person's time is very precious. It said that 25 to 30 minutes is a considerable amount of time to sit idle in a theatre watching unnecessary advertisements. It said people have tight schedules and do not have time to waste.

PVR INOX runs more than 900 screens across India and Sri Lanka.

He had 3 tickets and a bill, and he did not let it go.

JUST IN : SEBI PAPER ON CAS IS OUT

5 areas with 5 sets of proposals and a deadline for public comments of 3rd October

The full breakdown : 

A) F&O SETTLEMENT ON EXPIRY

Option 1: Blended VWAP
a. Last 30 mins of continuous cash trading + the 10 min CAS window
b. Weights based on actual traded value in each period

Option 2: Stay with CTS VWAP, for now
a. Only the last 30 mins of continuous cash trading
b. CAS trades play zero role in expiry settlement
c. Review a shift to Option 1 after at least a year, subject to liquidity and participation

B) MARKET TIMINGS

Option 1:
a. Normal cash trading in CAS stocks till 3:30 PM
b. CAS runs 3:31 to 3:40 PM
c. F&O stays open till 3:45 PM

Option 2:
a. Normal cash trading in CAS stocks till 3:15 PM
b. CAS runs 3:15 to 3:25 PM
c. F&O closes at 3:30 PM

Non-CAS stocks are not part of either option. They keep trading till 3:30 PM as they do today.

Two changes sit on top of both options: the CTS to CAS transition shrinks from 5 minutes to as little as 1 minute, and the post-CAS F&O window halves from 10 minutes to 5.

C) NO LIVE INDICATIVE INDEX DURING CAS

1. Stop disseminating the indicative index value through the CAS window
2. Stock-level indicative equilibrium prices continue as they are

SEBI's reasoning is simple -  A derived number was being read as a live index level and positions were being taken on it, when no such trade had happened.

D) CLAMPING DOWN ON ORDER SPOOFING

a. Overall CAS price band stays at plus or minus 3%
b. Orders within 1% of the reference price can still be cancelled
c. Orders placed beyond 1% cannot be cancelled at all, only modified in a price-improving direction

E) ICEBERG ORDERS ENTER CAS

a. Any unexecuted iceberg quantity at the end of continuous trading carries into CAS
b. It converts into a normal limit order with the full pending quantity disclosed in the CAS order book

Summary: SEBI wants the closing price to come from real orders instead of indicative signals, and wants expiry day settlement to stop being a guessing game

🔨 The Verdict: Demand order set aside for violation of the principles of natural justice. https://t.co/M2pF7gWdXu

📌 The Dispute
• The Assessee challenged the Show Cause Notice dated 19.11.2024 and the demand order dated 25.02.2025 on the ground that no opportunity of personal hearing had been granted.
• The Department fairly admitted that the Assessee had not been afforded an opportunity of hearing before passing the impugned order.

❓ Can a GST adjudication order be passed without granting a personal hearing when an adverse decision is contemplated?
⚖️ The Verdict:
No. The adjudication order was set aside for violation of natural justice, with liberty to the Department to pass a fresh order after granting due hearing.

🔹 The Dispute
Assessee: The Assessee challenged the order dated 30.03.2024, as no opportunity of personal hearing was granted before the adverse order was passed.
Department: The Department fairly admitted that no personal hearing had been afforded and agreed to pass a fresh order after providing due opportunity of hearing.

You can file a written complaint in the format of a simple letter, with the relevant points and your prayer, to the Registrar (Vigilance) of the same District Court.

You can write a grievance letter to the Chief Justice of the concerned State High Court.

Or you can write a grievance to the Chief Justice of India at the Supreme Court.

Or you can also right to Ministry of Law and Justice — Department of justice .

The Supreme Court has directed Anil Ambani and the Anil Ambani Group to file response (counter affidavit) on a public interest litigation (PIL) plea seeking a court-monitored investigation in a major bank fraud of nearly Rs 1.5 lakh crores. 

A bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi has also directed the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and the Enforcement Directorate (ED) to filed their respective status-reports over their ongoing investigation in the said fraud.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Seat Belts Are Not a Formality. They’re About Saving Lives. 🚗

A life-saving road-safety issue reaches the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India.

* A concern born from experience: As a doctor, researcher, and frequent traveller across India, I have repeatedly noticed rear-seat seat-belt buckles hidden beneath additional seat covers, making them difficult or impossible to use. When I ask drivers about this, I am often told, “Don’t worry, sir, the police only check the front seat.” But a seat belt is not for the police. It is for survival.
* Taking the issue to the Supreme Court: I am encouraged that the Hon’ble Supreme Court has taken up this important issue in the PIL I filed. My sincere gratitude to my advocate, Shri Wills Mathews, for presenting the matter before the Court.
* The Supreme Court’s message: The Bench comprising Hon’ble Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V. Mohana emphasized that seat belts are life-saving devices and stressed the importance of strict enforcement.
* The scale of the problem: Data cited in connection with the issue indicate that 16,025 people lost their lives in India in 2023 while not wearing seat belts, including 7,584 passengers.
* Rear-seat compliance is a serious concern: During the proceedings, the Court was informed that approximately 80% of car-occupant deaths in 2024 involved people who were not wearing seat belts, while rear-seat compliance was reportedly only around 5%.
* The hidden danger of seat covers: Many vehicle owners install additional seat covers that conceal the original seat-belt buckles and sockets. Over time, these mechanisms may become inaccessible, damaged, or rusted.
* The evidence is unequivocal: According to the World Health Organization, wearing a seat belt can reduce the risk of death among vehicle occupants by up to 50%.
* Prevention is the foundation of my work: As a diabetologist, I have dedicated my professional life to preventing complications rather than merely treating them. Many deaths from diabetes-related complications can be prevented. The same principle applies to road safety, basic precautions can save lives.
* From legal obligation to daily habit: I hope seat-belt enforcement will eventually become as routine and effective as helmet enforcement. The Supreme Court’s intervention is an important step towards ensuring that existing safety laws are implemented effectively.

Every seat must be a safe seat. Every journey must begin with safety.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

Why is NCPCR investigating Meta and Instagram?

Introduction

The issue exposes a critical tension between digital innovation and child protection, where platform-driven communication can become an unintended conduit for online child sexual exploitation.

Main Facts

A BBC investigation reportedly found paid Instagram advertisements promoting Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse Material (CSEAM) in India.

Although Meta prohibits such content, its automated moderation systems failed to detect every violative submission.

The Tech Transparency Project also identified CSEAM-related advertisements on Facebook and Instagram.

The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) summoned Meta officials and sought explanations.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) also questioned Meta.

Under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, NCPCR possesses powers resembling those of a civil court, including summoning persons and demanding information.

NCPCR’s mandate covers protection of children from abuse, exploitation and vulnerability.

Challenges

1. Algorithmic governance deficit: AI moderation cannot perfectly understand evolving abusive content.

2. Platform accountability: Corporate self-regulation may create gaps between stated policies and actual enforcement.

3. Cross-border jurisdiction: Global platforms complicate enforcement under domestic law.

4. Privacy–protection dilemma: Strong surveillance mechanisms must not undermine legitimate privacy.

5. Rapid technological adaptation: Predators continuously modify techniques to evade detection.

Constructive Criticism

The controversy demonstrates that merely prohibiting harmful content is insufficient. Platforms require proactive risk detection, transparent audits, rapid takedown mechanisms and institutional accountability. At the same time, regulation must remain proportionate and protect freedom of expression and privacy.

Way Forward

Establish independent algorithmic audits.

Strengthen platform transparency and accountability.

Create faster law-enforcement referral mechanisms.

Improve AI-based detection with human oversight.

Strengthen digital literacy and child-safety architecture.

Ensure coordinated action among NCPCR, MeitY, platforms and law-enforcement agencies.

Highlighted Keywords

CSEAM | Child Online Safety | Platform Accountability | Algorithmic Governance | AI Moderation | Digital Constitutionalism | Data Governance | Regulatory Oversight

Conclusion

Children’s digital rights require not merely safer platforms, but a robust ecosystem where technological capability is subordinated to constitutional morality, human dignity and the best interests of the child.

A solo Shopify operator just laid out his exact setup for running a store on $20 of Claude and pulling $10,478 in profit off $19,100 in monthly revenue. 

No team, no VAs, no agencies.

The math he opens with is the point. Running a store the "real" way costs $150 per product for a copywriter, $600 to $800 a month for a support VA, and $1,000 to $1,500 a month for a media buyer. Over $2,000 a month in overhead before a single person clicks Buy. It's why most stores die in month three.

His version: $20 Claude, $39 Shopify, six prompts.

He calls the six prompts his desktop. Each one does a job a human used to charge for.

research finds a recurring, annoying problem nobody has clearly solved yet. Priced $29 to $79, no single brand owning search results, before/after obvious in 5 seconds of silent video. The prompt forces Claude to cite sources or label every claim "[ASSUMPTION, verify]" so a guess never gets passed off as a fact.

supplier reads reviews like a detective and returns GREEN / YELLOW / RED / UNKNOWN with quoted evidence for every red flag. His first store died from a bad supplier. The product was fine, the shipping wasn't, disputes piled up, the payment processor froze the account. Now no supplier gets an order until this ten-minute check clears.

angle takes competitor listings and their 1 to 3 star reviews and finds the position none of them occupy. "Add reviews" and "better photos" are banned answers. If the complaint is "took 25 days," his page says exactly when it ships, in bold, near the top.

page rewrites AliExpress descriptions in the voice of a friend recommending something they actually use. Two versions, A/B tested. Any sentence that could appear on any product page for any product gets flagged and rewritten.

ad writes a 30-second vertical script as a 4-row shotlist with the exact words spoken. Banned phrases include "game changer," "you need this," "POV," "this changed my life." He films three versions in one evening changing only the first three seconds, runs each at $15/day for 48 hours, kills the two with weak hooks.

sunday runs every week for twenty minutes. Paste the numbers, get told what's broken in the first sentence, no encouragement, no "normal for this stage." Calculates break-even ROAS so he knows whether he's making money or burning it.

An offer prompt that raises AOV through bundles priced so margin goes up, not down. An iterate prompt that reads ad results and derives the next batch of hooks from what won, instead of testing more random angles.

Six to ten hours a week on the whole thing. Month one basically broke even. The store doesn't change, the prompts just get better at their jobs.

My take on the Bo Melton Vested Veteran Confusion:

I was out today busy from 9am until  just after midnight tonight with about 30 minutes of free time.  The Bo release news dropped about 10 minutes before I was able to check my phone for the first time and I was BLOWING UP!!

So getting caught up now - it's important to know there are technically two types of credited seasons.  One for minimum salary purposes, and one for benefits purposes.  Confusing, yes.  Almost always these two are identical, but as I will share below, super rare exceptions can occur causing misalignment.

In order to be a vested veteran for benefits (which is the measure for termination pay, retirement, waiver exemption, etc) a player needs 4 *benefit* credited seasons.

A *salary* credited season is earned by being on the 53-man roster (active/inactive) or elevated from the practice squad on gameday 3 times in a regular season (no playoffs).  IR, PUP, NFI, Exempt list do not count.

Bo Melton has exactly 3 *salary* credited seasons.  2023, 2024, 2025 all with the Packers.  This is not disputed.  NFLPA records show Bo as getting paid with the appropriate amount of credited seasons for each of these seasons, including 2026 now sitting with 3.

The interesting part - in 2022 the Packers signed Bo off of the Seahawks practice squad with 2 games left in the season.  As such he must be on the Packers 53 and paid for 3 games.  But there was only 2 games left of the season.

****Sooooooo - Melton did NOT earn a salary credited season for 2022.  However - people much smarter than me - have suggested the fact that he was in fact paid for 3 games, despite only being on the 53 for 2 games, probably led to a case between Bo, the NFLPA, and the NFL Management Council to argue he should have an additional *benefits* credited season to allow him to tap into the retirement/health/veteran benefits earlier than usually dictated.  These smarter people have been involved in these type of player dispute cases say these scenarios can happen --> creating a mismatch between *salary* and *benefit* credited seasons.

So in the end, while Bo Melton continues to have 3 credited seasons today in the 2026 season for salary purposes, he likely was awarded an additional 4th credited season for benefits purposes due to being paid 3 games for 2 games of services after likely arguing a case with the power holders between the NFL and NFLPA.

All to say.... It makes sense why the Packers were able to release Bo Melton earlier on Friday without having to be subject to waivers, despite showing as only have 3 credited salary seasons.

Super rare scenario - good on Brian Gutekunst & Russ Ball for taking advantage for whatever roster trick they have up their sleeves requiring Bo's former roster spot.

Now I'm going to bed - I have an even longer day tomorrow 8am - past midnight.

 Verify news & claims

 Verify images
Google Lens Search an image to find where else it has appeared and identify similar images.

TinEye Reverse-image search that can help identify older versions or the original source.

Verify videos & suspicious content

InVID/WeVerify Helps investigate videos, keyframes and images.

Wayback Machine Check older versions of webpages and see whether content has been changed or removed.

 Verify websites

Google Safe Browsing Check whether Google has flagged a website as dangerous.

My simple rule before posting
STOP → SEARCH → CROSS-CHECK → VERIFY → THEN SHARE.

Don't rely on a screenshot, WhatsApp forward, X post, or even a blue-check account as proof.

Find the original source and confirm the claim through at least one independent reliable source.

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

                              Bondage After Abolition

Fifty Years On, India's Bonded Labour Law Faces Its Hardest Test.

The law ended bonded labour in 1976. But debt, migration, poverty and coercion have kept reproducing the system, often far from public view.

By Premanand

Fifty years ago, India declared that no human being could be legally bound to labour because of a debt.

The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 did something unusually radical. It did not merely regulate bonded labour. It abolished the system itself. Existing bonded debts were extinguished. Agreements requiring bonded labour were declared void. Property connected to the bondage was to be freed. Every bonded labourer was legally released from the obligation to work.

The State was also given responsibility for finding those who remained trapped, freeing them and helping them rebuild their lives.

Yet the history of the five decades since the law was enacted exposes a disturbing contradiction.

India abolished bonded labour in law. It has not abolished the conditions that produce bondage.

The government itself continues to identify and rehabilitate people as bonded labourers. In its 2024–25 Annual Report, the Ministry of Labour and Employment reported that 3,16,336 bonded labourers had been released under the rehabilitation scheme up to 7 January 2025, with more than ₹1,062 crore released or reimbursed to states and Union Territories for rehabilitation.

That figure is not a measure of the total number of people living in bondage. It is a measure of those who entered the State's identification and rehabilitation system.

And that distinction may be the most important fact in understanding bonded labour in modern India.

The first problem: Who gets counted?

Bonded labour is an unusual crime because the State cannot prosecute what it does not first recognise.

A worker may be paid something and still be trapped.

A contractor may call an advance a loan.

An employer may describe withheld wages as an accounting dispute.

A worker may technically be free to leave but know that leaving means losing the advance, facing violence, abandoning family members or returning home with no livelihood.

The visible evidence of bondage may therefore be buried beneath apparently ordinary employment arrangements.

This is where the Supreme Court's interpretation of forced labour becomes crucial.

In People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India, the Court adopted a broad understanding of Article 23 of the Constitution. Forced labour, it held, cannot be reduced to situations involving physical chains or overt violence. Economic compulsion can also become a form of coercion.

The Court's approach has remained significant. In a 2026 judgment, the Supreme Court reiterated that " forced labour must be understood expansively and recognised that structural factors such as poverty can compel people to work against their will. It also referred to its earlier jurisprudence that payment below the statutory minimum wage can, in appropriate circumstances, trigger the protection of Article 23.

This changes the question investigators should ask.

Not simply:

"Was the worker physically forced?"

But:

"Did the worker have a genuine and meaningful ability to refuse or leave the work?"

That is a much harder question and one that requires serious investigation.

The new bondage does not always look like bondage

The traditional image of bonded labour is a landless agricultural worker permanently attached to a landlord because of an inherited family debt.

That system still has echoes in parts of rural India.

But contemporary bondage can be far more mobile.

A recruiter arrives in a village. An advance is offered. A family agrees to travel to another state for work. Transportation is arranged. The workers are told they will earn enough to repay the advance and take home a substantial amount of money.

The trap begins after they arrive.

The advance becomes a debt.

Food and accommodation are deducted.

The promised wage changes.

The period of employment is extended.

The accounts are controlled by the employer or contractor.

Identity documents may be withheld.

Leaving becomes difficult.

A worker who asks for payment may be told that the debt has not yet been cleared.

A family that arrived with an advance can therefore leave with nothing.

In extreme cases, workers are threatened or assaulted. Children may be made to work alongside adults. Women can face additional risks of sexual exploitation and violence; in some cases, during an emergency, the family involved in labour who have to go home are not allowed; if they are allowed, one family member is held as captive.

The precise form varies by industry and region.

The mechanism does not.

Debt becomes control.

Migration creates the perfect vulnerability

Modern bonded labour is closely connected to India's enormous informal and migrant labour economy.

A migrant worker often crosses not only a geographical border but an institutional one.

The worker leaves behind the local administration, community networks and social contacts that might otherwise provide protection. At the destination, the contractor may become the only person connecting the worker to employment, accommodation and transportation.

This dependence is particularly dangerous when the same intermediary also controls wages and the worker's debt.

The distance itself becomes a weapon.

A worker from one state may have difficulty communicating with police or labour officials in another. The worker may not know the local minimum wage. The worker may not know where to complain. A family may fear that approaching authorities will result in loss of employment or retaliation.

And if children are involved, the family may fear being separated.

This is how a labour arrangement can gradually become a system of control without ever resembling the historical image of a slave market.

Caste and poverty are not incidental

Bonded labour cannot be understood simply as a workplace violation.

It is also a manifestation of social inequality.

The Ministry of Labour has previously cited the National Commission on Rural Labour's finding that 86.6% of identified bonded labour belonged to Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe communities.

That historical figure matters because it demonstrates the deep connection between bonded labour and structural disadvantage.

Landlessness, caste discrimination, poverty, lack of secure employment and limited access to credit can leave certain communities disproportionately exposed to exploitative labour arrangements.

The same pattern can intersect with migration.

A worker with assets, savings and access to formal credit can usually negotiate differently from a worker who needs an advance simply to pay for food, travel or an emergency.

The advance that appears to be assistance can become the instrument through which bargaining power disappears.

That is why bonded labour is not merely about individual criminality.

It is about power.

The law puts responsibility on the State

The 1976 Act did not leave the problem entirely to the courts.

The Ministry says District Magistrates and Sub-Divisional Magistrates have statutory responsibilities under the Act, while vigilance committees are to be constituted at district and sub-divisional levels. Executive Magistrates can also exercise specified judicial powers for trying offences under the law.

This creates an important investigative question:

Are these institutions functioning as mechanisms of prevention, or only reacting after workers have already been rescued?

The difference is fundamental.

A functioning system would identify vulnerable workers before a crisis occurs. It would monitor recruitment networks, investigate high-risk workplaces, inspect suspicious labour arrangements and ensure that complaints are acted upon quickly.

A reactive system waits for a worker to escape, an activist to intervene, a journalist to report the case or a court to issue directions.

By then, the exploitation may have continued for months or years.

Rescue is only the beginning

There is another uncomfortable problem.

A worker can be legally freed and remain economically unfree.

The government recognises this through its rehabilitation scheme. Under the current scheme, financial assistance can range from ₹1 lakh for an adult male beneficiary to ₹2 lakh for specified vulnerable categories and ₹3 lakh in cases involving extreme deprivation or marginalisation. Immediate assistance of up to ₹30,000 can also be provided. District-level bonded labour rehabilitation funds are required to maintain a corpus for immediate assistance.

These provisions acknowledge something fundamental:

Freedom without livelihood is fragile.

Imagine a family rescued from a brick kiln.

The family returns home.

There is no land.

There is no secure employment.

The children have missed school.

The family has no savings.

The worker still needs food tomorrow.

Another recruiter arrives with an advance.

The cycle begins again.

This is why rehabilitation cannot be reduced to a cheque.

The real test is whether the family can survive without borrowing from another labour contractor.

The prosecution gap

The law also has a second weakness: the distance between identification and accountability.

Rescuing workers can produce an immediate and visible result. Prosecuting those responsible is slower, more complicated and dependent on evidence.

Who recruited the workers?

Who provided the advance?

Who controlled the accounts?

Who withheld the wages?

Who confiscated documents?

Who threatened the workers?

Who owned the workplace?

Who benefited financially?

In subcontracted industries, these questions can become remarkably difficult to answer.

The contractor may disappear.

The principal employer may claim ignorance.

Records may not exist.

Workers may be reluctant to testify.

The case can then be reduced to a dispute about wages rather than recognised as forced labour.

The government has acknowledged the prosecution challenge. In 2025, the Ministry said a Standard Operating Procedure had been issued to strengthen identification, rescue and prosecution, and that sensitisation and coordination with district officials were being undertaken to improve conviction rates.

The very existence of such measures is an admission that rescue alone has not solved the enforcement problem.

The accountability chain is only as strong as its weakest link

Bonded labour cases cross multiple departments.

Labour officials may be involved.

Police may be required to investigate.

District administration may be responsible for identification and rehabilitation.

Revenue officials may become relevant.

Child-protection authorities may be required where children are involved.

State governments have responsibilities under the Act.

The Union government provides the rehabilitation framework and financial assistance.

When these institutions fail to coordinate, the worker bears the cost.

This fragmentation can produce an especially dangerous illusion: everyone has responsibility, but no one feels responsible for the entire case.

A serious anti-bonded-labour system therefore needs a clear chain of accountability.

When a worker is identified, the question should not merely be whether the person was released.

Authorities should be able to answer:

Was the worker's debt extinguished?
Was immediate assistance provided?
Was the worker rehabilitated?
Was the employer prosecuted?
Was the contractor prosecuted?
Was the case investigated as forced labour where the evidence supported it?
Did the worker receive wages legally due?
Did the children return to school?
Did the family obtain sustainable livelihood support?
Did the family fall back into bondage?
Without these answers, "rescue" becomes a statistic rather than a measure of justice.

Fifty years of abolition and a continuing system
Government data provide an extraordinary historical warning. 

An official Ministry table records 2,95,962 bonded labourers identified and released under the earlier rehabilitation programme up to March 2013, with 2,76,101 recorded as rehabilitated. The numbers varied dramatically between states, with large numbers recorded historically in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.

The precise numbers should not be interpreted as a national prevalence survey.

They reveal something else.
Bonded labour has been repeatedly discovered after it was supposedly abolished.

That is the central contradiction.
If abolition had eliminated the underlying conditions, identification should have steadily moved toward zero.

Instead, the State continues to maintain a rehabilitation system, conduct surveys and issue procedures for identifying and prosecuting bonded labour.

The law survives because the problem survives.

The real investigation must follow the money

If India wants to understand modern bonded labour, it needs to investigate the economics behind it.

Who pays the advance?

Who recruits?

Who transports the workers?

Who controls the workplace?

Who determines the wage?

Who keeps the accounts?

Who receives the final product?

Who profits when labour costs are artificially suppressed?

These questions move the investigation beyond the individual contractor.

Bondage can persist because there is money to be made from it.

The cheaper the labour, the greater the incentive to maintain control over vulnerable workers.

This is particularly important in industries where production is fragmented through contractors and subcontractors.

A worker may be several contractual steps removed from the company or customer ultimately benefiting from the work.

That distance must not become a shield against responsibility.

What should the next fifty years look like?

India does not need another declaration that bonded labour is illegal.

That declaration was made half a century ago.

What India needs is an enforcement architecture capable of finding bondage before it becomes invisible.

That means regular, independent inspections of high-risk workplaces.

It means mapping recruitment corridors and labour contractors.

It means ensuring that migrant workers can access government services across state borders.

It means training police, labour officers and district officials to recognise economic coercion—not merely physical restraint.

It means protecting workers and witnesses who report bondage.

It means tracking prosecutions, convictions and rehabilitation outcomes rather than counting rescues alone.

It means ensuring that children rescued from forced labour return to education and do not simply move from one form of vulnerability to another.

And it means measuring rehabilitation by economic independence.

A worker who receives compensation but has no livelihood is not fully rehabilitated.

A family that escapes one contractor only to borrow from another has not truly escaped bondage.

The question India must answer

Fifty years ago, the law declared a profound principle: a debt cannot own a human being.

Today, the principle remains intact.

But in India's informal economy, debt can still determine where a person works, how long they work, how much they are paid and whether they can leave.

That is the modern face of bonded labour.

There may be no chain around the worker's ankle.

There may only be an advance.

There may be no locked gate.

There may only be a threat.

There may be no written contract.

There may only be an account book the worker cannot challenge.

There may be no visible violence.

There may only be the knowledge that returning home means hunger.

That is precisely why bonded labour is so difficult to eradicate.

It hides inside economic necessity.

The 1976 Act abolished the legal relationship.

The Constitution abolished forced labour as a fundamental wrong.

The Supreme Court has repeatedly insisted that freedom from forced labour must be interpreted in substance, not merely in form.

The remaining question is whether India's institutions will enforce that promise.

Because the ultimate test of abolition is not how many people the State has rescued.

It is whether vulnerable people can enter the labour market without surrendering their freedom.

Fifty years after abolition, that is the investigation India still has to complete.

@TeamYouTube this situation has gone way beyond a normal enforcement issue. On July 28, my channel started receiving an unusual wave of privacy complaints. Within roughly 3 days, 40+ complaints were filed against 41 completely unrelated videos, and 31 videos were removed. I appealed multiple removals and repeatedly contacted YouTube Support and Legal, but I never received a clear, case-specific explanation of the alleged privacy violations.

Then on August 14, the entire channel was terminated for Impersonation. I appealed and was rejected. When I contacted Creator Support, I was first told the termination was for Spam, despite the termination notice clearly stating Impersonation. The case was escalated, and I was then told the internal review confirmed Impersonation. I repeatedly asked a simple question: Who or what did I supposedly impersonate, and what exactly on the channel violated the policy? No specific answer was provided.

I submitted another official appeal through Google Form. It was confirmed as received and sent for specialized review, but that appeal has now also been rejected for Impersonation.

So after multiple reviews, I still haven't been told what specific person, channel, branding, video, or conduct supposedly constituted impersonation. I have never intentionally impersonated anyone or claimed to represent another creator or entity.

The matter is now pending before GAC in India and has also been brought to @SFLCin.

I am not asking for special treatment. I am asking for a fair, evidence-based review and a clear explanation of what actually happened. Please escalate this properly and reconsider the termination. @YouTube @UpdatesFromYT @YouTubeCreators @YouTubeIndia

Ray-Ban Meta glasses struck again. A woman walking home alone was secretly recorded by a man who approached her, then posted the footage on Instagram alongside similar clips of him doing this to other women, as part of "pickup" content.

She's filed a police complaint for stalking and voyeurism. IFF is assisting her with a legal notice to the creator, Instagram, and Meta, the second such notice against Meta in India.

This isn't a one off. It's a design problem.
Read more about it: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

A woman was followed, stopped on a dark street, secretly recorded through Ray-Ban Meta glasses and turned into an Instagram “pickup” reel that reached over 23 lakh views. Now, our legal notice seeks accountability from both him and Meta. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

The legal notice therefore puts Meta on notice not merely as the platform hosting the video, but as the designer, developer, manufacturer, marketer and seller of the glasses. It alleges negligence and product liability, arguing that Meta knew about the pattern of misuse but continued selling the device without an effective way for non-users or people being recorded to report that misuse. (9/10)

The notice seeks removal of every copy, preservation and disclosure of evidence, suspension of monetisation, an account of profits, an apology, and ₹2.05 crore in compensatory and exemplary damages. This case raises a larger question: when a company makes a camera that can be worn like ordinary glasses, who protects the person being recorded? Privacy cannot depend on whether the person being filmed has an Instagram account. (10/10)

The Supreme Court has closed India's Got Latent cases, but the question of an “Influencer Code” is not entirely over. On 14 August 2026, the Court quashed all FIRs arising from the episode and left the “larger issues” of regulating online speech for “another appropriate case”. Here is what that means. (1/7)

Read More: https://t.co/hecp2rl9W4

That qualifier matters. Executive action restricting speech must have a legal basis consistent with Article 19. The Court has previously held that executive instructions cannot independently impose restrictions on fundamental rights. The signed order also contains no finding that the content in question was obscene, nor does it establish a new standard for online speech. (6/7)

For now, there are no guidelines and no pending judicial direction requiring them. But MIB can still attempt regulatory changes, including through amendments to the IT Rules. If it does, IFF will insist on the public consultation promised to the Supreme Court, compliance with the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy and meaningful participation by affected creators and users. (7/7)

NIXI has changed its justification for suspending chalosansad dot in yet again. After first citing a “critical keyword”, and then relying on a 2004 policy clause that did not apply, it now invokes the Emblems Act and demands Central Government permission within seven days. On 8 September, IFF wrote back seeking a standstill and answers. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/2grOxR1bMy

The timing matters. The domain was suspended on 22 July. NIXI’s new legal opinion was obtained on 29 August, more than a month later and only after we challenged its earlier reasons. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that administrative action must stand or fall on the reasons given when the decision was made; authorities cannot ordinarily supplement an order with new reasons after it is challenged. (6/7)

NIXI has now also said that six other .in domains containing “Sansad”, along with other domains containing “Sansad”, “Parliament” or cognate expressions, will be examined. On 8 September, we asked NIXI for a 48-hour standstill on de-registration, deletion, transfer or reallocation of chalosansad dot in, confirmation of Aadhaar deletion, and disclosure of the correspondence it says raised concerns about publication. If no standstill is given, the registrant will approach the court. (7/7)

Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

NIXI has also given the registrant seven days to produce Central Government permission. Yet its reply identifies no ministry, officer, form, fee, procedure or timeline through which such permission can actually be obtained. We have therefore asked NIXI to explain the legal basis for this demand, and to provide the legal opinion dated 29 August on which its new position relies. (5/7)

quotedTweet.text:
On September 10th, 2013, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act, a vague law that was being used to arrest people for simply expressing dissent online.

11 years later, Maharashtra wants to bring it back in a new form, by amending the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for "online criminal defamation." But defamation is already covered under Section 356 of the BNS, and civil remedies already exist.

So why does the police need this new power? Recent FIRs against citizens and influencers for calling out potholes and infrastructure failures may hold the answer. We've fought this battle before. We don't need a new 66A with a new number.

text:
A 2:01-minute reel documenting villagers’ concerns over the proposed Google data centre in Visakhapatnam was blocked in India for 111 days. On 10 September 2026, it quietly came back online. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/TVxhdw9ZA1

The Sahyog route also raises a serious constitutional concern. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because the blocking framework contained procedural safeguards, including notice, hearing and a reasoned order. Section 79(3)(b), meanwhile, was read down to require a court order or government notification. A system that blocks first and explains nothing is difficult to reconcile with those safeguards. (9/10)

The reel is back, and we welcome that. But the questions remain unanswered, Who ordered the blocking? Why did the order name an unrelated person? Was a periodic review conducted? Why was the reel restored? IFF will continue seeking these answers from Andhra Pradesh authorities. Journalists should not need months of litigation to learn why their public-interest reporting was censored. (10/10)
